extracted.intended_audience: scientists, academic bloggers, and readers interested in science policy and research funding
extracted.subtask_description: Opinion and informational blog posts about science publishing, NIH budgeting and policy, academic metrics, and blogging/network editorial practices — aimed at informing and critiquing how science is funded, communicated, and evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blog network selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about who stays in a blog network involve a variety of factors, including frequency of posts and traffic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should make operational ground rules and protocols explicit (Blog Network Guidelines). News outlets have unique responsibilities to readers so their standards must differ from independent blogs; consider treating site-produced blogs as columns rather than unedited personal blogs. Adherence to network guidelines is implicitly a factor in retention decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improving a journal's (PLoS ONE) image within a field
rubrics_metrics.description: The pathway to improving PLoS ONE's reputation is via people who are seen as movers and shakers putting their respectable work there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target established, well-regarded senior researchers ('oldsters') to publish respectable work in the venue; relying on younger researchers or mid-career authors may not help and could risk further harm to reputation. Individual lobbying of respected figures is suggested as a (difficult) tactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using h-index and citation counts to judge scientific impact
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual's h-index and annual citation counts generate a gestalt impression of their impact, but may be skewed by outliers or atypical authorship patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of exceptions: a high h-index may be inflated by many middle-author contributions in a different, highly-cited domain; context and the nature of authorship should be considered rather than relying on a single metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH budget and prioritization criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations in appropriation reports suggest NIH should (a) pay attention to the age at which new investigators receive their first research grant, (b) ensure spending on specific diseases accounts for disease burden and death rates, and (c) prioritize federal funds for medical research over outreach and education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language in reports ranges from concrete to vague; specific numeric targets (e.g., for age of first R01) are stronger than 'urges.' Monitor whether previously 'tapped' funds are restored to NIH control and whether they are explicitly instructed to support young investigators; absence of explicit allocation weakens policy intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding budget 'tap' siphoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'tap' is a budget gimmick allowing HHS to shift money out of the NIH budget into other agencies; eliminating or restoring tapped funds to NIH is a criterion for protecting research funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If tapped amounts are returned to NIH (e.g., $700M returned as $715M), this can be a net gain — but the effect depends on whether funds are subsequently allocated to intended purposes (such as supplements for young investigators) and whether allocations are explicit rather than vague 'urges.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript prioritization categories
rubrics_metrics.description: A pragmatic categorization for choosing which paper to work on: (1) the paper I am working on, (2) the paper I should be working on as my top priority, (3) the paper I can't wait to work on once missing data arrive, (4) the paper I shouldn't bother working on until manuscripts under review return with comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list is a personal-priority rubric for time management; note that multiple items may refer to different stages of the same manuscript. Use this to sequence writing tasks realistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing witness credibility (legal/testimonial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Credibility of an eyewitness account depends on contemporaneous reporting, proximity to the event, absence of fabrication, and absence of a history of false claims or interfering with investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delayed contact with police, accounts that dovetail suspiciously with already-public versions, evidence of fabrication, prior criminal or deceptive behavior, and lack of independent corroboration all undermine credibility. Be skeptical of testimony that appears constructed after the fact or that matches a preferred narrative without independent support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial distinction between independent blogs and news outlet blogs
rubrics_metrics.description: A blog defined as 'the unedited voice of a person' suits independent bloggers, but news outlets must maintain different standards and responsibilities to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations should adopt explicit guidelines and may reframe staff blogs as columns with expectations around frequency, accuracy, and editorial oversight. 'Unedited' personal voice is less appropriate for outlet-branded content aimed at informing the public.
